summary_findings: THE NORTH-EAST WAS EXPECTED TO BE THIN AND IS THE RICHEST SINGLE PASS IN THIS DATABASE. The expectation was reasonable: tribal.json searched Hodson's Naga Tribes of Manipur for Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, pole star and constellation and got zero hits, and Gurdon's The Khasis yielded only the sun and the moon. But nobody had opened Lorrain's Dictionary of the Lushai Language (1940), and Lorrain is the best single source in this whole compilation. He has TWENTY-TWO STAR AND CONSTELLATION HEADWORDS, and for most of them he says which Western stars they are — Capella and three others in Auriga; a group in Taurus near Aldebaran; two close stars in Monoceros; Castor, Pollux, Procyon and Sirius; three small stars in Orion; Rigel; four stars in Delphinus; three in Aquila and four in Delphinus. No other source in this database maps an indigenous sky onto the modern one star by star, and Shakespear (1912) independently confirms that the system is real: 'Many of the stars and constellations have received names; most of them have some story attached to them.' THE FIGURES ARE NOT THE MAINLAND'S. There is no cot in Ursa Major and no thieves at it — the Mizo name Zâng-khua is not glossed at all, and what Lorrain records instead is ZÂNGKHUA BUNG-BU, a verb meaning 'to be upside down, as the Great Bear when high in the heavens', used metaphorically for the tables being turned. That is the only place in this database where a constellation's changing orientation has become an idiom, and it is a precise observation as well as a proverb. There is no plough in Orion and no deer: Si-mei-talh is 'three small stars in Orion' and Si-va-hluk is Rigel, neither glossed. The finest figure is DINGDI-PUAN-TAH — Capella at the apex of an isosceles triangle in Auriga is a young woman named Dingdi weaving, and the cloth she is weaving is pinned to the wall at the two base stars. A named character, an action, and two stars serving as nails: nothing else here is drawn in that much detail. TWO THREADS FROM THE EARLIER FILES CROSS THE MOUNTAINS. (1) STAR-DUNG. Mizo has the compound arsi êk, 'star-dung' — Lorrain's own entry for êk glosses it 'excrement, dung' and cross-refers here — but attaches it to the rosette markings on maturing bamboo rather than to a meteor, which is arsi thlâwk. Meitei puts it back where the Munda and Dravidian languages have it: thawānmicāk mathi, and Sharma prints the morphology himself, [star + faeces]. The idea now spans Munda, Dravidian and Tibeto-Burman. (2) THE PLEIADES RUN THE FARMING YEAR. SIRUK LA is the last and greatest nor'wester of spring, named because it coincides with the heliacal setting of the Pleiades, and the Lushais reckon the rice must be sown before it comes. That is the Santali ruhni, the Telugu kārte and the Rajasthani Bhaḍḍaḷī couplets again — and it also names a wind from a constellation, as Rajasthani okaṛa, dāvau and sūrayau do from Ursa Major. TWO NEW KINDS OF THING ENTER THE DATABASE HERE. SUK-CHEN, 'a pestle's length', is the unit in which the Lushai measure the height of the sun, moon or stars above the horizon — the first native angular measure recorded here, and the inland counterpart of the fist-and-finger measures of the west coast (kai kanakku, viral kanakku, dhru) that this database has not yet reached. And ĀWK, the fabulous creature that swallows the sun or moon, said by some to be the spirit of a Pawi chieftain — an eclipse-swallower who is not Rāhu. A THREE-LANGUAGE METEOR BELIEF, COMPARED BY THE ETHNOGRAPHER HIMSELF. Shakespear in 1912 records the Lushai CHAWIFA, a meteor that flies blazing through the village and kills the householder it lands on; gives the Lakher name THLA-SHI-PU for the same thing, with the opposite omen — where it falls is where to cut next year's jhum, and the crop will be good; and compares the Manipuri SANGAISEL. Sharma's Manipuri dictionary of 2006 has sanggāisen, 'meteor, shooting star', independently. Chawifa is NOT in Lorrain under that or any adjacent spelling, so for once the ethnographer has what the lexicographer lacks. NEGATIVE AND UNOBTAINED. Meitei has no name for Orion, the Great Bear, Venus or a comet in Sharma, and its only pole star is the Sanskrit dhrubatarā — so the Manipur valley looks far more Sanskritised than the hills around it, which is what its history would predict. No Naga, Garo, Bodo or Khasi material was added: Playfair's The Garos, Hutton's The Angami Nagas, Mills' The Ao Nagas and Endle's The Kacharis all returned HTTP 503 from archive.org across repeated attempts and were not read, and the mission dictionaries for those languages are not on DSAL. Hodson's Naga Tribes of Manipur remains, as tribal.json found it, empty of star names. Sylheti (Gwynn 2016, on DSAL) was not searched. The stories Shakespear says are attached to most Lushai constellations are not in Lorrain and are the obvious next thing to chase.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. arsi, p. 14
entries.quote: arsi, n . a star.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The contracted form si, 'a star', stands at p. 416 and is the first element of a dozen constellation names in this file.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. arsi thlâwk, p. 14
entries.quote: arsi thlâwk, n . a shooting star. arsi ´ thlâwk, arsi ´ thlawh, v . to shoot, as a star.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The verb stands at the same headword: a star does not fall in Mizo, it shoots.

entries.sky_object: star (generic), in the compound arsi êk 'star-dung'
entries.usage_note: Lorrain's entry for êk (p. 122) glosses it 'excrement, dung, manure' and cross-refers to arsi êk among its compounds, so the literal sense is his and not the compiler's.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. arsi êk, p. 14
entries.quote: arsi êk, n . the greyish rosette-like markings found on certain bamboos—generally regarded as an indication of their maturity or durability.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. THE STAR-DUNG IDEA, IN A TIBETO-BURMAN LANGUAGE AND ON A NEW OBJECT. tribal.json traced meteors-as-star-excrement through Santali ipil ic', Mundari ipilko ic' and Gondi sukum pelkta; tribal_fieldwork.json added Kolam Suka erengten and the Korku. Mizo has the compound but attaches it not to a meteor — which is arsi thlâwk — but to the rosette markings that appear on bamboo as it matures. The Meitei entry in this file has the same compound back on the meteor, with the recorder's own morphological analysis to prove it.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-ruk, p. 419
entries.quote: Si-ruk, n . the Pleiades.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The name is transparent as si 'star' plus ruk, but Lorrain glosses no second element and none is claimed here.

entries.sky_object: the nor'wester that blows at the heliacal setting of the Pleiades
entries.usage_note: The rule is agricultural: sow the rice before the Siruk la.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Siruk la, p. 419
entries.quote: Siruk la, n . the last and greatest of the north-west hurricanes or nor'-westers of spring, so named because it synchronizes more or less with the heliacal setting of the Pleiades. The Lushais reckon that their rice-crops should be sown before this hurricane and its accompanying rain takes place.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A PLEIADES SOWING RULE, AND THE ONE THAT NAMES A WIND. This database already had the Pleiades governing the farming year in Santali ruhni, the Telugu kārte and the Rajasthani Bhaḍḍaḷī couplets, and it had winds named from a constellation in Rajasthani okaṛa, dāvau and sūrayau. Mizo does both at once, and Lorrain states the astronomy exactly — a heliacal setting, not a rising.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Zâng-khua, p. 558
entries.quote: Zâng-khua, (zâng-khaw), n . the constellation of Ursa Major or the Great Bear; also called in English the Plough, and King Charles' Wain or Waggon.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. No cot, no thieves, no bier. Every mainland community in this database reads these seven stars as a piece of furniture with someone stealing it; the Mizo name is not glossed at all by Lorrain, and the figure he records instead is about the constellation's ORIENTATION — see Zângkhua bung-bu below.

entries.sky_object: Ursa Major, standing on its head
entries.usage_note: A verb, not a noun, and in ordinary speech a proverb about reversal of fortune.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Zângkhua bung-bu, p. 559
entries.quote: Zângkhua ´ bung-bu, (—bung-but), v . to be upside down as the Great Bear constellation when high in the heavens. Metaphorically used for 'the tables being turned'. ( Zângkhua a bungbu ta = The tables have been turned. Zângkhua a la bungbu ang = The tables will yet be turned, or, Things will be altered or reversed some day.)
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. THE ONLY PLACE IN THIS DATABASE WHERE A CONSTELLATION'S CHANGING ORIENTATION HAS BECOME AN IDIOM. Nothing else here turns the sky into a figure of speech about the world turning over. It is also a precise observation: at these latitudes the Dipper does invert as it crosses the meridian.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. khawi-dâng, p. 254
entries.quote: khawi-dâng, n . 1. a wasp. 2. the name of a star in the constellation of the Great Bear.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Lorrain does not say which star, so none is claimed. Homonym warning: the primary sense of the word is a wasp.

entries.sky_object: a triangle of four stars in Auriga

modern_star.common_name: a triangle of four stars in Auriga, the brightest being α Aurigae

entries.usage_note: The figure is a scene indoors: a named girl at her loom, with the cloth pinned to the wall at two points that are themselves stars.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Dingdi-puan-tah, p. 116
entries.quote: Dingdi-puan-tah, n . the name of a Lushai constellation comprising Capella and three other stars in Auriga which form an isosceles triangle. The star at the apex of the triangle represents a young woman named Dingdi engaged in weaving a cloth which is affixed to the wall at the two points marked by the base stars.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. THE BEST-DRAWN FIGURE IN THIS DATABASE. Most sky-figures elsewhere here are a single object — a cot, a plough, a deer. This one has a named character, an action, and two stars doing duty as nails in a wall. Compare the Kolam Mahua tree at Crux with an old woman and a young woman gathering flowers beneath it, in tribal_fieldwork.json: both are domestic scenes rather than emblems, and neither has any counterpart in the Sanskrit sky.

entries.usage_note: Khiangte is the name of a Lushai clan, given at the immediately preceding headword.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Khiangte Zâwng-zîm, p. 263
entries.quote: Khiangte Zâwng-zîm, n . the name of a constellation: a group of stars in Taurus, near Aldebaran.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A constellation named for a clan. Nothing else in this database attaches a lineage name to a group of stars.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Nufa Thembu Inchuh, p. 345
entries.quote: Nufa Thembu Inchuh, n . the name given to two stars in close proximity to one another in the Unicorn constellation.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. 'The Unicorn constellation' is Monoceros. Inchuh is Lorrain's word for a mutual or reciprocal action; nu-fa is mother-and-child. No fuller gloss is given and none is invented.

entries.sky_object: a bow-shaped figure spanning Gemini and the two Dog constellations

modern_star.common_name: a bow-shaped figure of five or more stars
modern_star.bayer: α and β Geminorum with stars to the south of them

entries.usage_note: Lorrain names the stars: Castor and Pollux in Gemini, Procyon in Canis Minor, Sirius, and a few others. The first element vân-pui is the great vault overhead.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Vân-pui Sai-hrua, p. 544
entries.quote: Vân-pui Sai-hrua, n . the name of a constellation—a bow-like configuration formed by Castor and Pollox in Gemini, Procyon in Canis Minor, Sirius, and a few other stars.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A figure drawn ACROSS three modern constellations, which is what makes Lorrain's list worth having: he maps the Lushai sky onto the Western one star by star instead of assuming they divide it the same way.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-mei-talh, p. 418
entries.quote: Si-mei-talh, n . the name of a Lushai constellation comprising three small stars in Orion.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Almost certainly the Belt, but Lorrain says only 'three small stars in Orion' and the Belt stars are not small, so the identification is graded 'likely' and left out of modern_star. Note what is NOT here: no plough, no yoke, no seed drill, no deer. The mainland reading of Orion does not reach the Lushai Hills.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-va-hluk, p. 419
entries.quote: Si-va-hluk, n . the name of a star—Rigel (in Orion).
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Compare Mundari siṭan ipil 'the ploughman' and Korku Doba 1 'the first bullock' for the same star in tribal.json and tribal_fieldwork.json — three unrelated languages, three unrelated readings.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-chak-ai, p. 417
entries.quote: Si-chak-ai, n . the name of a Lushai constellation comprising a certain cluster of nebulae and two stars. [and, p. 416] Si-aia, n . the name of a Lushai constellation of stars, also called Sichakai, which see.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Two headwords for one figure, cross-referred by Lorrain. A 'cluster of nebulae' visible to the naked eye is most likely a rich Milky Way star-cloud, but Lorrain does not say where it is and nothing is claimed.

entries.quote: Si-hnawk-khur, n . the name of a Lushai constellation comprising four stars in Delphin.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Lorrain's 'Delphin' is Delphinus. Four stars there is Job's Coffin, the little diamond that is the whole of the constellation to the naked eye.

entries.usage_note: Lorrain gives two senses at one headword: the planet Mars, and Betelgeuse. One name for the two conspicuous red objects in the sky, planet and star alike.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Si-kei-sen, p. 417
entries.quote: Si-kei-sen, n . 1. the planet Mars. 2. Betelgeux. (Same as Sisakei. ) [and, p. 419] Si-sakei, n . 1. the planet Mars. 2. Betelgeux. (Same as Sikeisen. )
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A RED-STAR CATEGORY RATHER THAN A NAME FOR ONE BODY. Tamil cem-mīṉ 'the red star' does the same job in this database, covering Mars and Arundhatī, and Malayalam has ceṅṅāyi. Mizo, Tamil and Malayalam are unrelated; the category is the sky's, not the language's.

entries.usage_note: Lorrain's indî, 'to be in conjunction, especially as the planets Jupiter and Venus' (p. 198), shows the two were watched together.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Hrâng-chhuana, p. 179
entries.quote: Hrâng-chhuana, n . Jupiter; the planet Jupiter.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Hrângchhuana is a hero of Lushai story; the planet carries his name.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Chawng-mawii, p. 66
entries.quote: Chawng-mawii, n . the evening star; Venus as the evening star. (See Vârparh. )
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A woman's name — mawi is 'beautiful' — set against the morning star's Vâr-parh, which is a description of daybreak. The pair is Lorrain's own cross-reference.

entries.literal_meaning: vâr is 'dawn, to be light'; parh is 'to blossom, to spread'
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Vâr-parh, p. 545
entries.quote: Vâr-parh, n . the morning star; the day star; Venus as the morning star.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The dawn breaking open. Lorrain's neighbouring entries vâr ṭian 'early dawn' and khawvâr ṭian carry the same root.

entries.usage_note: thlasik is the cold season; kawng is a road. The neighbouring headwords are thlasik ni kîr 'the winter solstice' and thlasik tui hnawt chhuaktu, the rain that warms the rivers at the end of the cold season.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. thlasik kawng, p. 479
entries.quote: thlasik kawng, n . the Milky-way.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. THE ROAD AGAIN, AND DATED TO A SEASON. Every mainland community in this database makes the Milky Way a road — of cattle, of the dead, of animals — and the Nicobarese make it water. Mizo makes it a road too, but names it for the time of year when it stands overhead, which no other language here does.

entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. si-mei-khu, p. 418
entries.quote: si-mei-khu, n . a comet.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. Lorrain glosses only 'a comet'; the elements are separately his and the reading of the compound is the compiler's, which is why it is in literal_meaning and not in the quote. Compare Sanskrit dhūmaketu 'smoke-banner', the same image reached independently.

entries.sky_object: a unit of measure for the altitude of the sun, moon or stars above the horizon
entries.usage_note: Lorrain's example sentence is a traveller judging whether the village is reachable before dark.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. suk-chen, p. 421
entries.quote: suk-chen, n . the height or length of a pestle. (Used to indicate the height of the sun, moon, or stars above the horizon, either before setting or after rising.) Ni sukchen a la awm, kan la ban ang = The sun is still the height of a pestle above the horizon, we shall reach (the village tonight).
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. A NATIVE ANGULAR MEASURE, and the first in this database. The maritime traditions of the west coast measure star altitudes in fists and fingers — kai kanakku in Lakshadweep and Malabar, viral kanakku in Tamil Nadu, dhru in Gujarat — and this is the inland counterpart, reckoned from the household pestle. It creates the object 'Measuring the sky' in this database, which the maritime wave will fill.

entries.sky_object: the creature that swallows the sun or moon at an eclipse
entries.usage_note: The verb is impersonal and takes the creature as subject: 'the Āwk eclipses the sun'.
entries.citation: J. Herbert Lorrain, Dictionary of the Lushai Language, Bibliotheca Indica Work No. 261 (Calcutta: The Asiatic Society, 1940), s.v. Āwk, p. 20
entries.quote: Āwk, n . the name of a fabulous creature which is supposed to swallow the sun or moon at the time of an eclipse. Some say that the awk is the spirit of a Pawi chieftain. Āwkin a lem, Āwkin ni a lem, Āwkin thla a lem. [and] âwk lem, n . an eclipse; ni âwk lem, a solar eclipse; thla âwk lem, a lunar eclipse.
entries.notes: Lorrain's dictionary is public domain (he died in 1944) and is quoted verbatim from DSAL's page view. The Indian eclipse-swallower is Rāhu everywhere in the Sanskritic material; the Mizo one is a named local ghost, the spirit of a Pawi chief. Creates the object 'Eclipses' in this database, which had none.

entries.sky_object: a meteor that kills the householder it falls on
entries.citation: J. Shakespear, The Lushei Kuki Clans (London: Macmillan, 1912), V. Folklore, p. 105
entries.quote: The Lushais speak confidently of "Chawifa," and many say they have seen it. They describe it as a kind of meteor, which flies through the village blazing brightly, and if it alights on a house the owner must die.
entries.notes: Shakespear's Lushei Kuki Clans is public domain and is quoted verbatim from the archive.org full text. NOT IN LORRAIN: the dictionary has no chawifa headword under that or any adjacent spelling, so this belief is attested by the ethnographer and not by the lexicographer — worth stating, because the rest of the Mizo material in this file is the other way round. Shakespear himself compares the Lakher Thla-shi-pu and the Manipuri Sangaisel, both entered below; the three-language comparison is his, made in 1912, and Sharma's Manipuri dictionary of 2006 independently confirms the third of them.

entries.sky_object: a meteor, and an omen of where to cut the jhum
entries.region: the Lakher country, southern Lushai Hills (now southern Mizoram)
entries.usage_note: Where it falls is where next year's swidden should be cut.
entries.citation: J. Shakespear, The Lushei Kuki Clans (London: Macmillan, 1912), Part II (the Lakhers), p. 205
entries.quote: The Lushai Chawifa is known as "Thla-shi-pu," and if it falls in the jungle that is the place to cut your jhum, for then you are sure of a good crop. It seems that Thla-shi-pu is merely a meteor; the Lakhers have not surrounded this natural phenomenon with the myths which the more imaginative Lushais delight in.
entries.notes: The same object as the Mizo Chawifa and the opposite omen: for the Lushai it kills the householder, for the Lakher it marks good ground. Shakespear's own editorial aside — that the Lakhers have not surrounded the phenomenon with myths, unlike 'the more imaginative Lushais' — is the kind of judgement tribal.json already flags in Rivers, Man and Hoffmann, and is not reproduced in the entry. The page is given as Shakespear numbers Part II; his Lakher section is separately paginated in some printings and the running head was used.

entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. thawānmicāk, p. 86
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. The base of the meteor compound below.

entries.usage_note: Sharma prints the morphological analysis himself: thawanmicak 'star' + mathi 'faeces'.
entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. thawānmicāk mathi, p. 86
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. THE STAR-DUNG THREAD, CONFIRMED BY THE RECORDER'S OWN MORPHOLOGY. Santali ipil ic', Mundari ipilko ic', Gondi sukum pelkta, Kolam Suka erengten and the Korku all have it (tribal.json, tribal_fieldwork.json); Mizo has the compound on bamboo markings instead. Meitei puts it back on the meteor and, uniquely among all of them, the lexicographer breaks the compound down in print so the reading rests on his analysis and not on the compiler's. Munda, Dravidian and now Tibeto-Burman.

entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. sanggāisen, p. 188
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. A second Meitei word for the same thing, and the one Shakespear cites from Manipur in 1912 as 'Sangaisel', comparing it to the Lushai Chawifa and the Lakher Thla-shi-pu. A 1912 ethnographer's aside and a 2006 dictionary agreeing on a word is about as good as corroboration gets in this database.

entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. khongjomnubi, p. 54
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. Marked 'Astron.' by Sharma. The final element nubi is 'woman, girl'; the whole is not glossed and no reading of it is claimed here.

entries.usage_note: Sharma gives the morphology: ningthou 'king' + turel 'stream'.
entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. ningthou turel, p. 105
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. A RIVER, NOT A ROAD. Every mainland community in this database makes the Milky Way a road; the Nicobarese make it a spring of water; the Mizo, two hundred miles away, make it the winter road. Meitei makes it a king's river — the Sanskritic Ākāśagaṅgā reached independently, or so it looks, since Sharma gives no loan etymology and the elements are both Meitei.

entries.citation: H. Surmangol Sharma, Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (Imphal, 2006), s.v. dhrubatarā, p. 97
entries.notes: Sharma's Learners' Manipuri-English Dictionary (2006) is in copyright: the finding is paraphrased and `quote` is null, as with the field surveys in tribal_fieldwork.json. The Meitei Mayek script and the roman are as DSAL prints them. Sanskrit Dhruva-tārā in Meitei script and phonology — the one clearly Sanskritic item in the whole north-eastern file, and it names the one star the indigenous systems here do not.

caveats: Lorrain (1940) is public domain — he died in 1944 — and is quoted verbatim throughout, from DSAL's page view rather than its search view. Shakespear (1912) is public domain and is quoted from the archive.org full text. Sharma (2006) is in copyright: the seven Meitei entries are paraphrased and their `quote` is null, on the footing this database uses for the field surveys.

TEN OF THE TWENTY-NINE MIZO ENTRIES ARE GRADED `unidentified`, and that is the honest shape of the source. Lorrain names a figure and then, about a third of the time, says nothing further than 'the name of a Lushai constellation'. Those entries are kept rather than dropped — an unidentified indigenous figure is a result, and the number of them is itself the finding, since no other language in this database has anything like twenty-two named sky figures. Where Lorrain gives Western stars they are reproduced exactly; where he does not, `modern_star` says so in words and nothing is guessed.

Si-mei-talh is graded `likely` rather than `certain` for a reason worth stating: 'three small stars in Orion' is almost certainly the Belt, but the Belt stars are second-magnitude and not small, so the identification may be wrong and the Bayer letters are deliberately left out of modern_star.

Literal meanings are given only where Lorrain glosses the elements at their own headwords. arsi êk rests on his entry for êk (p. 122), which cross-refers to it; si-mei-khu is marked as the compiler's reading of elements Lorrain glosses separately, which is why it is in `literal_meaning` and not in the quote. Si-ruk, Zâng-khua, Si-archang, Si-kawi-kâp and the rest are left unglossed, because a transparent-looking Mizo compound is not evidence of anything without the dictionary saying so.

One printed error is reproduced as printed: Si-archang's gloss reads 'arranged in an are resembling the curve of a cock's tail feathers', where 'are' is a compositor's error for 'arc'. The quote is as DSAL renders the page and the correction is stated in the entry's notes.

The Lakher entry's page reference is soft. Shakespear's Part II on the Lakhers is separately paginated in some printings, and the page here is taken from the running head of the archive.org scan used; the entry is graded `likely` on that account, not because the reading is in doubt.

Two entries carry no vernacular name at all. The general statement from Shakespear that 'many of the stars and constellations have received names' is entered as a source-level fact because it is the independent corroboration that Lorrain's list is a system and not a lexicographer's miscellany. The precedent is the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entry in tribal.json and the four name-less entries in tribal_fieldwork.json.

Register is `tribal` throughout except Meitei dhrubatarā, which is `sanskritic` — Sanskrit Dhruva-tārā in Meitei script. Calling the Mizo material `tribal` rather than `vernacular` follows this database's use of the tag for a distinct non-Sanskritic tradition, not a judgement about the Mizo as a community; the same tag covers Santali, Mundari and Nicobarese here.

The north-east is far from finished. Playfair on the Garos, Hutton on the Angami and Sema, Mills on the Ao, Lotha and Rengma, and Endle on the Kacharis were all requested from archive.org and all returned HTTP 503; the mission dictionaries for Garo, Bodo, Ao and Angami are not on DSAL and were not reached by other routes. Sylheti was not searched. Khasi still rests on the five words Nissor Singh's dictionary gave tribal.json.
